title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extracellular bacteria. Antibodies neutralise toxins and opsonise; complement lyses; phagocytes destroy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intracellular bacteria. Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ and TNF to activate macrophages; cytotoxic lysis of infected cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antifungal immunity. Wall glycans and mannans activate innate cells and the alternative complement pathway; Th17 IL-17 recruits neutrophils and antimicrobial peptides.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Helminths. Th2 IL-4 and IL-5 drive IgE, mast cell and eosinophil degranulation (major basic protein), ADCC.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Protozoa. Intracellular protozoa need Th1; extracellular ones are handled by antibodies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antiviral immunity. Type I interferons create an antiviral state; NK and CD8 T cells kill infected cells; antibodies neutralise free virus.

title: Three levels and two ways of anti-infectious immunity?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: Three levels and two ways of anti-infectious immunity?
body.back: Prevent entry, eliminate quickly, control multiplication; innate and adaptive.
Th1 (IL-12, T-bet, STAT-4): IFN-γ, intracellular. Th2 (IL-4, GATA-3, STAT-6): extracellular. Th17 (TGF-β + IL-6, RORγt, STAT-3): fungi, extracellular. Treg (TGF-β, FoxP3).
IFN-I (PKR, OAS/RNase L, Mx), NK and CD8 cytotoxicity, neutralising antibodies, complement, ADCC.
Type I: IFN-α, β. Type II: IFN-γ. Type III: IFN-λ (IL-28A, IL-28B, IL-29).
Extracellular: antibodies, complement, phagocytes. Intracellular: Th1 IFN-γ/TNF-activated macrophages, cytotoxicity.
Capsule (pneumococcus), polysaccharides (gonococcus), blocked fusion (M. tuberculosis), phagosome lysis (Listeria), resistant wall (M. leprae), lipoarabinomannan.
Intracellular protozoa: Th1. Extracellular protozoa: antibodies. Helminths: Th2, IgE, mast cells, eosinophils (MBP), ADCC.
Wall glycans activate innate cells and alternative complement; Th17 IL-17 boosts neutrophils and antimicrobial peptides.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antigen. Any molecule inducing an immune response and reacting specifically with its products (antibody, BCR, TCR); usually several epitopes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hapten-carrier conjugate. Bound to a protein carrier, the hapten induces anti-hapten and anti-carrier antibodies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Epitope. The part bound by the paratope of an antibody or receptor; linear (continuous) or conformational (discontinuous).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hapten. Low molecular weight antigen (one epitope) that cannot trigger a response alone.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immunogenicity. All immunogens are antigens, but not all antigens are immunogens.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Superantigens. Staphylococcal enterotoxins, TSS toxin: activate many T cells at once, causing massive IL-2, TNF-α, IFN-γ release.
Any natural, artificial or synthetic molecule that induces an immune response and reacts specifically with its products (antibody, BCR, TCR).
Antigenicity: recognition by immune effectors. Immunogenicity: ability to trigger a response in vivo. All immunogens are antigens, not the reverse.
Foreignness, size (> 3-5 kDa), rigidity, complexity, chemical nature, host genes (MHC II), dose, route.
Binds paratope; 1-3 nm, 15-18 aa or 5-6 sugars; linear or conformational; antigen = mosaic of epitopes.
B: native antigen via membrane Ig. T: processed peptide presented by MHC on APCs.
Small single-epitope molecule, antigenic but not immunogenic; immunogenic when bound to a carrier.
Staph enterotoxins, TSS toxin: polyclonal T activation, massive IL-2, TNF-α, IFN-γ.
Allo: within species (ABO). Xeno: between species. Auto: self.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adaptive lymphocytes. B cells make antibodies; CD4 helper, CD8 cytotoxic, regulatory T cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Granulocytes. Neutrophils (60% of WBC, 36 h, phagocytosis), eosinophils (2-5%, allergy and parasites), basophils (< 1%, histamine, heparin; mast cells in tissues).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hematopoietic stem cell. Pluripotent, self-renewing; gives lymphoid and myeloid progenitors; 10¹¹-10¹² blood cells a day.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lymphoid progenitor. Regulates adaptive immunity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Monocytes/macrophages and others. Phagocytic antigen-presenting cells; also erythrocytes and megakaryocytes (platelets).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Myeloid progenitor. First responders to infection.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Innate-like lymphocytes. NK (no TCR/BCR), NKT (NK + T markers, liver), γδ T cells (epithelia), at the innate-adaptive interface.
Pluripotent, self-renewing; gives lymphoid and myeloid progenitors; 10¹¹-10¹² cells/day.
Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils/mast cells), monocytes/macrophages, dendritic cells, erythrocytes, megakaryocytes.
Neutrophils ~60% (phagocytosis), eosinophils 2-5% (allergy, parasites), basophils < 1% (histamine, immediate hypersensitivity).
HLA-DR (antigen presentation), lysozyme, lysosomal hydrolases, TNF, IL-1 (fever, acute phase).
Natural cytotoxicity (perforin/granzyme, Fas-L, TRAIL), ADCC via Fc receptor, cytokines (IFN-γ).
NKT: NK + T markers, conserved TCR, liver. γδ T: epithelia, limited repertoire, not classical-MHC restricted.
B cells (antibodies), CD4 helper T, CD8 cytotoxic T, regulatory T.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alternative pathway. Spontaneous C3 activation on microbial surfaces, amplified by factors B and D, stabilised by properdin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: C3 convertase. Classical/lectin C4b2a; alternative C3bBb; cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: C5 convertase. C4b2a3b (or C3bBb3b) cleaves C5 into C5a and C5b.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Classical pathway. Triggered mainly by C1q binding antigen-bound IgM or IgG; C1s cleaves C4 and C2.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Other effects. C3a and C5a (anaphylatoxins) drive inflammation and chemotaxis; C3b opsonises for phagocytosis and clears immune complexes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lectin pathway. Mannose-binding lectin with MASP proteases recognises microbial carbohydrates; resembles the classical pathway.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Membrane attack complex. C5b recruits C6, C7, C8 and polymerised C9, forming a pore that lyses the pathogen.
~35 proteins (12 effectors), protease cascade; lysis, inflammation, opsonisation, virus neutralisation, immune complex clearance.
Birth: half adult level; 2-14 y: higher; adult ~3 g/L; liver makes 95%; half-life 24 h; rises in inflammation.
C2, C4, factor B in MHC class III (chromosome 6); deficits mostly classical pathway and MAC.
C1q binds IgM/IgG-antigen → C1r, C1s → C4, C2 → C3 convertase C4b2a → C5 convertase C4b2a3b.
MBL + MASP bind microbial carbohydrates, then cleave C4 and C2 like C1.
Spontaneous C3b on microbes + factor B (cleaved by D) → C3bBb stabilised by properdin; amplification.
C5b + C6 + C7 insert, C8, polymerised C9 → MAC pore → lysis.
C3a, C4a, C5a: inflammation, chemotaxis. C3b: opsonisation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Signal 1. Specific recognition of peptide presented by MHC class II on the APC.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Signal 2. Membrane co-stimulatory molecules; without it the T cell is not activated.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Signal 3. Cytokines from the APC orient the naive Th0 cell.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Th1. Induced by IL-12; secretes IL-2 and IFN-γ; cellular immunity against intracellular pathogens.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Th2. Secretes IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13; humoral immunity against extracellular pathogens.
One receptor per lymphocyte; specific antigen binding → clonal expansion → effector and memory cells.
Initiation (APC-T), clonal expansion (Th-B, Th-T), effector (Th1, Th2, CTL).
1: TCR + peptide-MHC. 2: co-stimulation. 3: cytokines that polarise.
Early: phosphorylation cascades. Late: gene transcription (NF-κB, NFAT).
Th1 (IL-12): IL-2, IFN-γ, cellular immunity, intracellular pathogens. Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, humoral immunity, extracellular pathogens.
Polysaccharides (LPS), polymeric proteins; BCR cross-linking; IgM, no switch, low affinity, no memory.
B cell presents peptide on MHC II → Th help via CD40L-CD40 + cytokines → class switching, affinity maturation, memory.
Heavy-chain constant region rearrangement: same Fv specificity, different Fc effector function.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fab fragments. Variable domains (VH, VL); hypervariable loops (CDR1-3) on a framework contact the epitope.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fc fragment. Constant domains: binding to effector cells, complement fixation, placental transfer, catabolism.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Heavy chains. Define the class; 4 domains (5 in IgM and IgE).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hinge. Papain digestion gives 2 Fab + 1 Fc.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Light chains. Kappa or lambda; one variable and one constant domain.
Same molecule: 'Ig' describes structure, 'antibody' describes function.
2 heavy + 2 light chains; domains ~110 aa (heavy 4, IgM/IgE 5; light 2); variable and constant regions.
Fab (×2): variable domains recognising epitopes. Fc: effector functions (Fc receptors, complement, placenta, catabolism).
Conserved framework supports hypervariable loops (CDR1-3) at the tip that contact antigen and create diversity.
Pentamer + J chain, ~10% serum Ig, first in primary response, best classical complement activator, no placental transfer.
Main serum Ig; 4 subclasses; half-life ~3 weeks; crosses placenta; opsonisation (FcγR), ADCC (FcγRIII).
~12% serum; monomer in serum; secretory dimer with J chain and secretory component; mucosal immunity; IgA1 serum, IgA2 secretions.
IgD: B-cell receptor, 0.25% serum, no known effector role. IgE: trace, mast cells/basophils, allergy and parasites.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adhesion. Leukocyte integrins bind Ig-superfamily adhesion molecules on endothelium; the cell flattens.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Targeted chemokines. IL-8 (CXCL8) attracts neutrophils, MCP-1 monocytes, eotaxin eosinophils; leukotrienes, prostaglandins and anaphylatoxins also recruit.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diapedesis. The leukocyte squeezes between endothelial cells into the tissue.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Migration. It crawls through the matrix toward the injury, guided by chemotactic factors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rolling. Selectins on activated endothelium slow leukocytes, which roll along the vessel wall.
Response of living vascularised tissue to aggression; non-specific defence that heals and restores homeostasis.
Physical, chemical, infectious, immune (allergy), tissue necrosis.
Circulating and resident cells; mediators: cytokines, histamine, complement, lipid mediators, kinins.
Small glycoprotein messengers acting on receptors; autocrine, paracrine, endocrine; from Th cells and macrophages.

title: Four phases of the inflammatory response?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: Four phases of the inflammatory response?
body.back: Initiation (vascular, platelets), amplification (recruitment), stabilisation, resolution/repair (pro-resolving mediators).
Rolling (selectins), adhesion (integrins/Ig superfamily), diapedesis, migration (chemokines).
IL-8 → neutrophils; MCP-1 → monocytes; eotaxin → eosinophils.

title: Cardinal signs and phases of acute inflammation?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: Cardinal signs and phases of acute inflammation?
body.back: Redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function; vascular, cellular, resolution phases.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cells. Phagocytes and innate-like lymphocytes recognising conserved microbial patterns.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antimicrobial molecules. Lysozyme breaks bacterial walls; lactoferrin chelates iron; cationic defensins and cathelicidins form pores; surfactant proteins act as opsonins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Humoral components. Complement (~30 proteins, three pathways) and cytokines such as interferons.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mechanical barriers. Skin delays entry and its acidity inhibits growth; mucus traps microbes and cilia sweep them out.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Commensal flora. Competes with pathogens, blocks the epithelium, makes antibacterial substances, helps digestion and immune maturation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Physiological barriers. Body temperature and gastric acidity kill or restrain microbes.
Innate: rapid (hours), non-specific, constant. Adaptive: slow (days-weeks), specific repertoire, improves with exposure.
Barriers, non-specific chemical agents (complement, cytokines), non-specific effector cells.
Skin (pH 3-5), mucus and cilia; temperature, gastric acidity.
Lysozyme (walls), lactoferrin (iron), defensins, cathelicidins (LL-37), surfactant SP-A/SP-D (opsonins), interferons.
12-50 aa, cationic; pores in membranes, interfere with DNA/RNA/protein synthesis; α-defensins (neutrophils, Paneth cells), β-defensins (epithelia).
Metabolism (vitamins, fatty acids), competition and colicins against pathogens, immune maturation.
Balance of activating and inhibitory (KIR → MHC I) receptors; kill missing self, modified self, allogeneic cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Circulation. Blood and lymphatic vessels connect all lymphoid organs into one network.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bone marrow. Primary organ: stem-cell reservoir, B-cell maturation with BCR gene rearrangement and negative selection; houses plasma cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lymph nodes. ~1,000 reniform nodes filtering lymph; cortex (B follicles), paracortex (T cells), medulla.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: MALT. Mucosal defence (digestive GALT, bronchial BALT); mainly secretory IgA.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spleen. Filters blood; protects the vascular compartment; IgG and IgM responses.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thymus. Primary organ in the anterior mediastinum: T-cell maturation, positive (cortex) and negative (medulla) selection.
Primary: bone marrow (B), thymus (T): maturation and selection. Secondary: lymph nodes, spleen, MALT: antigen encounter and immune responses.
Stem-cell reservoir, B-cell maturation, home of plasma cells.
Diversity from few genes, cell-specific receptor, irreversible and inherited.
Self-reactive BCR → receptor editing → apoptosis; ~95% die; less strict than thymic selection.
Positive (cortex): TCR recognises self-MHC → MHC restriction. Negative (medulla): high-affinity self-recognition → apoptosis → tolerance.
Hormones peak at puberty then fall; fibro-fatty replacement; memory T cells maintain numbers.
Systemic (spleen, lymph nodes): IgG, IgM. Mucosal (MALT: GALT, BALT): secretory IgA.
Cortex: B-cell follicles (primary, secondary). Paracortex: T cells. Medulla.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Endogenous antigens. Proteins made inside the cell, such as viral or tumour proteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Exogenous antigens. Captured by phagocytosis, pinocytosis or receptor-mediated endocytosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Class II pathway. Degraded in endosomes/lysosomes; peptides longer than 13 amino acids loaded onto MHC II.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: MHC class I. On all nucleated cells; 'designates cells to destroy' to CD8 cytotoxic T cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: MHC class II. Mainly on antigen-presenting cells; 'designates cells to activate' via CD4 helper T cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Class I pathway. Degraded by the proteasome; peptides of 8-10 amino acids loaded onto MHC I.
Region of >200 highly polymorphic genes whose products present antigen and cause graft rejection; HLA in humans.
All nucleated cells; α chain + β2-microglobulin; endogenous peptides (8-10 aa) to CD8 T cells.
Mainly APCs; α + β chains; exogenous peptides (>13 aa) to CD4 T cells.
Complement and inflammation-related proteins.
Most polymorphic genes; HLA-A/B/C (I), DR/DP/DQ (II); codominant; haplotype inheritance.
Sentinels in skin, lung, gut; capture (phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptors), process, mature, migrate to lymphoid organs, present to naive T cells.
Endogenous: proteasome → ER → MHC I → CD8. Exogenous: endosome/lysosome → MHC II → CD4.
1: TCR + peptide-MHC. 2: B7-CD28, CD40-CD40L. 3: cytokines (IL-12). Signal 1 alone → anergy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Capture. Receptors bind microbes directly or through opsonins: IgG (Fc receptors) and C3b (complement receptors).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chemotaxis. Phagocytes follow gradients of bacterial N-formyl peptides, PAF, leukotriene B4, anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a) and chemokines.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Destruction. The phagosome fuses with lysosomes; debris is released by exocytosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Engulfment. Actin polymerisation extends pseudopods around the particle, forming a phagosome.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oxygen-independent killing. Granule enzymes (proteases active at neutral pH, lysozyme), cationic antimicrobial proteins, lactoferrin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oxygen-dependent killing. Respiratory burst: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide, then H₂O₂ and hydroxyl radicals; nitric oxide synthase makes reactive nitrogen species.
Ingestion and degradation of particles > 0.5 µm by phagocytes; opsonins (IgG1/3, C3b) coat targets to enhance uptake.
Granulocytes (mainly neutrophils) and mononuclear phagocytes (monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells).
15 µm, 3-5 lobes, first line; FcγR, CR1, CR3; secrete IL-8, IL-1, IL-12, TNF-α.
Monocytes (2-5% of WBC) leave blood after ~8 h; macrophages larger, more enzymes, tissue-specific.
Phagocytosis (scavenger), immune modulation (cytokines, prostaglandins), antigen presentation.
Chemotaxis, capture, engulfment (actin, phagosome), destruction (phagolysosome).
Dependent: NADPH oxidase ROS, NO synthase RNS. Independent: granule enzymes, cationic proteins, lactoferrin.
Neutrophils release DNA-histone traps with myeloperoxidase, elastase, gelatinase, lactoferrin; requires elastase; induced by microbes, immune complexes, cytokines.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Agglutination. Antigens on particles (red cells, bacteria, latex) are linked into clumps; direct (ABO) or via anti-globulin (Coombs).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immunoenzymology. Enzyme converts a colourless substrate into a coloured product read as optical density; includes ELISA and Western blot.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immunofluorescence. Fluorochrome-labelled antibody; read under a fluorescence microscope or by flow cytometry; under 3 hours.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Precipitation. Soluble antigen and antibody form a visible precipitate, maximal in the equivalence zone; done in liquid or gel.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Radioimmunoassay. Radioactive isotope label; rarely used today.
Epitope-paratope binding with steric complementarity; non-covalent forces; forms an immune complex.
Directly visible: precipitation, agglutination. Labelled: immunofluorescence, immunoenzymology (ELISA, Western blot), radioimmunology.
Oudin (simple), Mancini (radial, quantitative), Ouchterlony (double), immunoelectrophoresis.
Direct: ABO grouping. Artificial: Coombs test (autoimmune haemolysis, transfusion, newborn haemolytic disease).
Fluorochrome label; direct or indirect; fluorescence microscope or flow cytometry; < 3 h.
Direct (antigen), indirect (antibody, e.g. anti-HIV), sandwich; enzyme + substrate → optical density.
SDS denaturation, PAGE separation by mass, transfer to nitrocellulose, patient serum, enzyme-linked secondary antibody, substrate.
ELISA, repeat ELISA if positive, then Western blot confirmation (ELISA false positives).
